summary: Describes the Verizon Wireless procedure for distributing and updating Mobile IP cryptographic keys in cdma2000 networks, including 1xEV-DO. It runs between the mobile node and a key distribution function. This memo is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A phone on a mobile network needs secret keys to roam safely. This describes one company's way of handing the phone a fresh key when the old one needs changing.

questions: how does dmu distribute mobile ip keys
what is the dynamic mobile ip key update procedure
how does rsa encryption protect dmu messages
subtitle: A secure way to update cryptographic keys in mobile networks.

tldr.problem: Mobile devices in cdma2000 networks need secure ways to update their cryptographic keys without complex infrastructure.
tldr.mechanism: The Dynamic Mobile IP Key Update (DMU) procedure uses RSA public key encryption to securely distribute fresh keys from the network to mobile devices, with mutual authentication between device and network.
tldr.outcome: Devices can efficiently receive updated keys with less computational overhead than Diffie-Hellman key exchange, and are protected against certain false base station attacks.

today: RFC 4784 is an Informational RFC that documents an existing Verizon Wireless procedure. It remains informational and has not been obsoleted, so it describes a system deployed in cdma2000 networks.

sections.title: The Problem and Solution
sections.content:
Mobile nodes (phones and modems) in cdma2000 networks need secure cryptographic keys for Mobile IP authentication. RFC 4784 describes the Dynamic Mobile IP Key Update (DMU) procedure, developed by Verizon Wireless, which securely distributes and updates these keys between a mobile node and the network's RADIUS Authentication, Authorization and Accounting (AAA) Server.

The procedure uses RSA public key cryptography. Each mobile node is pre-loaded with the service provider's RSA public key during manufacturing. When a key update is needed, the mobile node generates new secret keys locally, encrypts them using the RSA public key, and sends them to the network. Only the AAA Server, which holds the corresponding private key, can decrypt and extract the new keys.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone comes with a public key built in. When it needs fresh keys, it scrambles them using that key and sends them to the network. Only the network has the special key to unscramble them. This way, the keys stay secret during delivery.

sections.title: The Key Exchange Format
sections.content:
The encrypted key data, called MIP_Key_Data, contains four main components. The most important is the encrypted payload holding three 128-bit keys: the MN_AAAH key (for mobile node to AAA authentication), the MN_HA key (for home agent communication), and the CHAP_key (for Simple IP authentication). The payload also includes two authenticators: an AAA_Authenticator (a 64-bit random number the mobile node invents, to verify the AAA Server really decrypts the message) and an MN_Authenticator (a 24-bit random number for extra authentication in certain networks).

The MIP_Key_Data payload is appended to the mobile node's Mobile IP Registration Request as a vendor-specific extension, then forwarded from the Packet Data Serving Node (PDSN) to the AAA Server as a RADIUS Vendor-Specific Attribute. With 1024-bit RSA encryption, the total payload is 132 bytes: 128 bytes encrypted plus a 4-byte Public Key Identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: The scrambled message contains three secret keys and two special numbers the phone made up. The network checks that one of those numbers comes back to prove it really was the network doing the unscrambling, not an imposter.

sections.title: The Key Update Process
sections.content:
The DMU procedure involves multiple steps between the mobile node, the PDSN (which acts as a Mobile IP Foreign Agent), and the AAA Server. First, the mobile node sends a standard Mobile IP Registration Request. The AAA Server checks its policy and, if a key update is required, sends an Access Reject message (via the PDSN) with the MIP_Key_Update_Request attribute. This tells the mobile node which public key to use for encryption. The mobile node then generates new keys and the two authenticators, encrypts them with the designated public key, and sends a new Registration Request containing the encrypted MIP_Key_Data.

The AAA Server receives the encrypted payload, uses its RSA private key to decrypt it, and verifies the mobile node's authentication. If verification succeeds, the AAA Server returns the AAA_Authenticator to the mobile node (in an Access Reject message). The mobile node checks that this returned value matches the authenticator it sent, confirming the network can decrypt its messages. Once confirmed, both the mobile node and network commit the new keys to permanent storage and proceed to the Home Agent for final registration completion.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone sends a request to the network. If the network says it needs new keys, the phone makes up fresh keys and two magic numbers, scrambles them, and sends them back. The network unscrambles them, then sends one of those magic numbers back. If the phone sees its own magic number come back, it knows a real network (not an attacker) did the unscrambling.

sections.title: Security and Robustness
sections.content:
The DMU procedure provides mutual authentication. The mobile node authenticates the AAA Server through RSA encryption: only the legitimate AAA Server can decrypt the AAA_Authenticator and return it correctly. The AAA Server authenticates the mobile node through established cdma2000 1X authentication (for devices with an Authentication Key and Shared Secret Data) or optionally via the MN_Authenticator for 1xEV-DO networks where radio access network authentication is not available.

The procedure includes state management to handle network failures. The AAA Server tracks each subscription in one of three states: KEYS_VALID, UPDATE_KEYS, or KEYS_UPDATED. If messages are lost during the exchange, the mobile node and network can recover by resynchronizing their states, allowing the mobile node to retransmit the same encrypted payload without fear that stale credentials will be accepted.
sections.plainLanguage: Both the phone and the network check each other. The phone knows the network is real by verifying the magic number comes back. The network checks the phone is real through existing authentication or an extra password. The system remembers where it is in the update process, so if messages get lost, it can try again without confusion.

sections.title: RADIUS and Mobile IP Extensions
sections.content:
RFC 4784 defines four new RADIUS Vendor-Specific Attributes and four corresponding Mobile IP Vendor-Specific Extensions to carry DMU messages. The MIP_Key_Update_Request attribute (Vendor-Type 1) tells the mobile node which public key to use. The MIP_Key_Data attribute (Vendor-Type 2) carries the encrypted key material and Public Key Identifier. The AAA_Authenticator attribute (Vendor-Type 3) contains the decrypted authenticator returned by the AAA Server. The Public_Key_Invalid attribute (Vendor-Type 4) signals that the public key the mobile node used is no longer valid, requiring a new key update with a different public key.

A Public Key Identifier structure identifies which public key is being used. It includes the Public Key Organization Identifier (PKOID) for the key creator, an organization index (PKOI) to distinguish different key pairs, an expansion field for future use, and an Algorithm Type and Version (ATV) field indicating the encryption strength (such as RSA with 1024-bit, 768-bit, or 2048-bit modulus).
sections.plainLanguage: The network and phone exchange four types of messages. The first says which scrambling code to use. The second carries the scrambled keys. The third proves the network decrypted the message. The fourth says the scrambling code is broken and try another one. Each message labels which scrambling code was used and how strong it is.
